segments.note: Like the Beechview line, the Overbrook streetcar route used the Mount Washington Transit Tunnel (opened Dec 1904) to reach Downtown from the South Hills, running a separate, parallel alignment through Overbrook rather than Beechview. Frequency estimated, unsourced.
sources: VERIFIED 2026-08-24: the Mount Washington Transit Tunnel opened Dec 1 1904 and carried its first fare-paying passengers Dec 4 1904 — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Washington_Transit_Tunnel
Headway remains an estimate — the era boundary is verified, the service frequency is not.

segments.note: Retained by the Port Authority after its 1964 takeover of Pittsburgh Railways as one of the surviving private-right-of-way South Hills lines. Frequency estimated, unsourced.
sources: VERIFIED 2026-08-24: "On March 1, 1964, the system was acquired by the newly established Port Authority of Allegheny County" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Light_Rail
Headway remains an estimate — the era boundary is verified, the service frequency is not.

segments.note: Converted to modern light rail as part of Stage I (1984-87), giving the Overbrook corridor a through route to the new Downtown Subway and (from 1987) South Hills Village. The deteriorating line was suspended in 1993 pending a full rebuild -- a real service gap, not a data gap -- with no direct rail service until it reopened.
sources: VERIFIED 2026-08-24: Stage I construction "began on December 10, 1980" and "the first modern light rail cars began operating on April 15, 1984" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Light_Rail
Headway remains an estimate — the era boundary is verified, the service frequency is not.

segments.note: The rebuilt Overbrook line reopened in June 2004 (a $386 million project with 28 new light rail vehicles) after 11 years closed, restoring through service to Downtown.
sources: VERIFIED 2026-08-24: "The Overbrook line reopened in June 2004" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Light_Rail
Headway remains an estimate — the era boundary is verified, the service frequency is not.

segments.note: Extended under the Allegheny River to North Side/Allegheny via the North Shore Connector (opened Mar 25 2012). Formally branded the Blue Line in the 2020 color-coded renaming.
sources: VERIFIED 2026-08-24: the North Shore Connector "opened to the public on March 25, 2012, with a final cost of $523.4 million" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Light_Rail
Headway remains an estimate — the era boundary is verified, the service frequency is not.

metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.

metadata.not_yet_sourced: Per-segment verification pass 2026-08-24: 5 of 5 segment boundaries in this file are verified against the Pittsburgh Light Rail article, the Mount Washington Transit Tunnel article or the Post-Gazette report of the 2020 renaming, each quoted in the segment's own sources entry. The 1987–2012 span is an editorial division rather than a documented change, and is marked as such.
